The glossary (https://leanprover-community.github.io/glossary.html) defines propositional, definitional, syntactical equalities, which are usually what one sees.
However, somewhere in Lean source code, one also encounters structural equality and alpha equivalence. What are they? (Assume they refer to a consistent term)
(See the documentation of guard_target for example.)
There's also "alpha equality" (… might be a typo?), and definitional equality is also distinguished between "reducible definitional equality" and "default definitional equality", making things a bit more confusing.

Context: I come across this while reading a comment in show explaining what it does and how it differs from type ascription. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/master/src/Lean/Elab/BuiltinNotation.lean#L137
Alpha equivalence means renaming bound variables, e.g. (fun a : Nat ↦ 3) ≡ₐ (fun b : Nat ↦ 3), and (∀ foo : Nat, True) ≡ₐ (∀ bar : Nat, True)

Alpha equivalence is also a reduction step you could take, similar to beta reduction.
See here for documentation about other types of reductions. Strangely this doesn't mention alpha; perhaps because Lean uses De Bruijn indices under the hood (docs#Lean.Expr.bvar) so we don't have to worry about it.
Needless to say the glossary accepts pull requests to improve it too

user202729 said:

definitional equality is also distinguished between "reducible definitional equality" and "default definitional equality"

This is about the concepts known as "reducibility" and "transparency" if you've ever come across these terms. Unfortunately I don't think we have great learning resources for it yet, but essentially: checking when two expressions are definitionally-equal is hard (undecidable), so some parts in Lean don't want to try too hard because it makes things faster.
So definitions are marked with a reducibility level, and parts of meta code use varying  transparency modes (kept in the monad state). When checking for definitional equality, Lean checks the transparency mode to see which definitions it should unfold (based on their reducibility).

(not sure if this is in the kernel or just in the meta code; there are two separate defeq algorithms technically)

This affects various things in practice, but they're easier to understand if you play around with Lean and experience them for yourselves (and possibly ask questions on Zulip). btw abbrev marks a definition as reducible, and semireducible is the default.
Reducibility is an implementation detail and not about the type theory itself
@Chris Bailey https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/3a685e6c855f0eb4ccabe92e21120f1b1ef81d24/src/Init/Guard.lean#L83 it says "default defeq".
in this case it means definitional equality at default transparency
